name: Scansion-Void
specific_features: Surface so cratered that no original terrain remains
Thin layer of metallic micrometeorite dust
description: Scansion-Void is a tiny barren body so thoroughly bombarded by micrometeorites over its lifetime that no original surface terrain survives. Every square meter has been pitted, pulverized, and re-pitted until the entire world is covered in a uniform layer of regolith created from its own shattered crust. Exposed bedrock scarps where ancient impacts excavated deeper than usual provide the only geological variety, their faces displaying the composition of the original world beneath its self-made shroud of dust.

Without atmosphere, the surface exists in the raw vacuum of space, each micrometeorite arriving at full velocity without any ablation to slow it. The accumulation of metallic dust from billions of years of impacts has created a thin surface layer with an unusually high concentration of rare elements, a treasure spread so thin across such vast area that it resists economical collection. The planet glitters faintly in direct sunlight, the metallic dust lending it an appearance of tarnished silver.

The regularity of the regolith layer has made Scansion-Void useful as a calibration reference for geological survey instruments. Its uniformity provides a known baseline against which sensor readings can be verified, a function that has made this otherwise unremarkable body a standard waypoint for survey vessels. The irony is not lost on the crews: a world destroyed by bombardment finding purpose as a measuring stick for the study of other worlds.

No permanent installation exists on Scansion-Void, its negligible gravity and lack of resources making it unsuitable for anything more than brief instrument calibration stops. The micro-gravity environment means surface operations are essentially spacewalks with slightly more solid footing, and the metallic dust has a tendency to cling to equipment via static charge, requiring decontamination procedures after every surface excursion. The planet persists as it has for billions of years, patiently absorbing the universe's debris and converting it into a coat of shining dust.
